summary: The smallest country on the African mainland, stretched in a narrow strip along both banks of the Gambia River and surrounded on three sides by Senegal; it became independent from Britain in 1965.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam came to the Gambia River valley between the 11th and 13th centuries with merchants and the power of the Mali Empire, but at first it was mostly followed by rulers and traders. In the "Soninke–Marabout wars" from the mid-19th century to the 1890s, Muslim religious leaders (marabouts) overthrew the traditional non-Muslim rulers, spreading Islam throughout the country. Today most people belong to Sufi orders such as the Tijaniyya and Qadiriyya, and religious leaders have great influence in society.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In 1816 Britain founded Bathurst (today's Banjul) at the mouth of the Gambia River, Methodist missionaries followed in 1821, and the Catholic Church also set up schools in turn. Christians are mainly the Aku people of the Banjul area (descendants of freed slaves) and some Serer and Jola; although few in number, the mission schools had a profound influence on education.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Traditional beliefs are found mainly among peoples such as the Jola in the west; among them, the Mandinka "Kankurang" masked initiation rite was proclaimed a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity by UNESCO in 2005, and such traditional customs are also often retained by Muslims.

religion.background: The Gambia River valley fell within the sphere of influence of the Mali Empire in the Middle Ages, and Islam was introduced by merchants and scholars, but it did not become the faith of the majority until the religious wars of the 19th century. Britain founded a colonial base at the river mouth in 1816, bringing Christian missions and mission schools. After independence in 1965 the Gambia adopted a secular constitution; in 2015 the former president Jammeh declared it an Islamic republic, but a new government withdrew this in 2017, and Islam, Christianity and traditional customs have long coexisted in harmony.

ranking.name: Mandinka
ranking.description: The Mandinka entered the Gambia River valley in the 13th century as the Mali Empire expanded westward, and later founded polities such as the Kingdom of Kaabu. The Mandinka are the largest ethnic group in the Gambia, so Mandinka is one of the most widely spoken languages, and the epics that griots (hereditary singer-storytellers) sing to the kora are also handed down in it.

ranking.name: Fula
ranking.description: The Fula were originally nomadic people of the West African savanna; in the 19th century the Fula leader Alfa Molo founded the Kingdom of Fuladu on the upper Gambia River, spreading Fula in the eastern region. Many Fula are still engaged in livestock herding.

ranking.name: Wolof
ranking.description: Wolof comes from neighboring Senegal, and the Jolof Empire of the 14th–16th centuries made it a dominant regional language. In the Gambia the Wolof are not the largest group, but Wolof is the lingua franca of the capital Banjul and the urban areas, and many people of different ethnic groups use it in markets and daily life.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: In 1816 Britain founded a colony at the mouth of the Gambia River, which became a separate colony in 1888 and remained so until independence in 1965. English thus became the official language and the language of education, government and media, but most people learn it at school, and very few have English as a mother tongue.

language.history: The Gambia's indigenous languages belong to the Atlantic and Mande branches of the Niger–Congo family, and include Mandinka, Fula, Wolof, Jola and Serer. The medieval Mali Empire made Mandinka the main language of the valley, and the expansion of the Fula and Wolof in the 19th century changed the distribution of languages. British colonization made English the administrative language, and being surrounded by French-speaking Senegal makes the Gambia an English-speaking island in a Francophone region. Today Wolof is growing in influence in the cities and has become the de facto lingua franca.

ranking.name: Peanut stew (domoda)
ranking.description: A thick stew of chicken or beef simmered with peanut butter, tomato, onion and vegetables such as pumpkin and sweet potato; the flavor is rich, and it is eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: Peanuts are native to South America and were brought to West Africa by the Portuguese in the 16th century. From the 1830s the British colony of the Gambia began exporting peanuts in large quantities, and peanuts became the most important cash crop, remaining one of the Gambia's main exports to this day. Peanut stew has thus become the Gambia's national dish, called domoda in Mandinka, and is the most common lunch in every household.

ranking.name: Benachin
ranking.description: Rice cooked in one pot with fish or meat, tomato, onion, eggplant, cassava and other vegetables; the rice turns red and absorbs the flavor of the ingredients.
ranking.history: The name means "one pot" in Wolof, and shares its origin with Senegal's jollof rice, going back to the Jolof Empire founded by the Wolof in the 14th–16th centuries. It reflects the rice-based food tradition of the Senegambia region and spread across West Africa with trade and migration. In the Gambia it is often made in large pots at religious festivals, weddings and family gatherings.

ranking.name: Yassa (lemon-onion chicken)
ranking.description: Chicken or fish is marinated in plenty of onion, lemon juice and mustard, grilled, and then stewed with the onion sauce; it is tangy and appetizing and is eaten with white rice.
ranking.history: Yassa originates in the nearby Casamance region of southern Senegal, where the Jola season with citrus and onion, and with close contact between peoples of the Gambia and Casamance, the dish became a Gambian home dish. It is common at festivals and banquets, and the version made with fish is a specialty of the coastal region.

ranking.name: Okra and palm oil soup (soupekanja)
ranking.description: A thick soup boiled from okra, red palm oil, dried or smoked fish and chili, sometimes with seafood or beef added, often poured over white rice.
ranking.history: Okra is native to Africa and palm oil is the traditional cooking oil of West Africa, and the combination of the two is an ancient feature of West African cuisine. The "kanja" in the name is okra in Wolof, while the first half derives from "soup" (French soupe), reflecting the blending of local and colonial languages. The soup is common in Mandinka and Jola households and represents the Gambian everyday diet based on fish and vegetables.

ranking.name: Yogurt millet dessert (churai/thiakry)
ranking.description: Millet flour is steamed into small grains and mixed into sweetened yogurt or sour milk, flavored with nutmeg, vanilla and raisins, and eaten chilled as a dessert.
ranking.history: Millet is one of the oldest staple grains of the West African Sahel, and its drought tolerance suits the local climate. This dessert shares its origin with Senegal's "thiakry" and is traditionally made for occasions such as Eid al-Adha (Tobaski), baby naming ceremonies and weddings to serve guests who come to give congratulations. It is one of the most popular cooling desserts for Gambians in hot weather.
